[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]

== Biography ==
=== Early life and family ===

Adam Dickie Glasgow was born in 1815 at Ballymena, County Antrim, Ireland. He was the son of [[Glasgow-1657|John Glasgow]] and [[McClure-6341|Jane McClure]].

His brother [[Glasgow-1780|James McClure Glasgow]] repeatedly referred to Adam as “my brother Adam” in his missionary journal.<ref name="JamesJournal">[https://revjamesmcclureglasgow.blogspot.com/ James McClure Glasgow missionary journal], first-person journal repeatedly identifying Adam as James’s brother and tracing his movements from Belfast to New Zealand (accessed 17 July 2026).</ref>

The surname and middle name appear with variant spellings in later records, including '''Adam Dickey Glasgow'''.

=== Ministry and missionary work ===

Adam was a Presbyterian minister.

A published history of Knox Church, Dunedin, states that he was born at Ballymena in 1815 and later joined his brother, Dr. James McClure Glasgow, in India.<ref name="KnoxHistory">[https://archive.org/details/historyofgreatam02myer ''History of Knox Church, Dunedin''], account identifying Adam Dickey Glasgow as born at Ballymena, Ulster, in 1815 and stating that he joined his brother Dr. Glasgow in India (accessed 17 July 2026).</ref>

James’s journal initially places Adam in Belfast. Later entries report his arrival in New Zealand and his connection with a congregation in Dunedin.<ref name="JamesJournal" />

=== Emigration to New Zealand ===

Adam emigrated from Ireland to New Zealand about 1861.

His burial record states that he had lived in New Zealand for two years at the time of his death. His last address was Dunedin, and his occupation was recorded as minister.

=== Death and burial ===

Adam died at Dunedin, Otago, New Zealand, on '''18 March 1863''', aged 48.

His death was registered in New Zealand in 1863 under the name Adam Dickie Glasgow.<ref name="NZDeath">New Zealand Births, Deaths and Marriages, death registration 1863/2037, Adam Dickie Glasgow, aged 48.</ref>

He was buried at Dunedin Northern Cemetery, Dunedin, in Block 25, Plot 3.<ref name="FindAGrave">Find a Grave, memorial for Adam Dickey Glasgow, 1815–18 March 1863, Dunedin Northern Cemetery, Dunedin, Otago, New Zealand; burial details record Block 25, Plot 3, occupation minister, native of Ireland, two years in New Zealand, and death at Dunedin.</ref>

=== Identity ===

Adam Dickie Glasgow belonged to the nineteenth-century Glasgow family of Ballymena.

The evidence distinguishing him includes:

* his birth at Ballymena in 1815;
* his identification by [[Glasgow-1780|James McClure Glasgow]] as his brother;
* his earlier residence in Belfast;
* his connection with James in India;
* his migration to New Zealand;
* his Presbyterian ministry in Dunedin;
* his death there in 1863.

He should not be conflated with Adam Glasgow of Inishrush, who was born about 1758.

The two men belong to different generations and families. Adam Dickie Glasgow should therefore not be used to connect the Ballymena family to the earlier Inishrush family or to create an unsupported relationship with Robert Glasgow of the Victorian period.

=== Name spelling ===

The profile uses '''Adam Dickie Glasgow''', matching the New Zealand death registration.

The spelling '''Adam Dickey Glasgow''' appears in the burial memorial and published sources. Both spellings refer to the same man.

=== Further research ===

Useful additional records may include:

* Adam’s baptismal record at Ballymena;
* Presbyterian ordination and ministerial records in Ireland;
* records of his time with James in India;
* passenger or immigration records for his journey to New Zealand;
* Dunedin church records;
* a contemporary obituary or death notice;
* his original New Zealand death certificate.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. Adam D. Glasgow of Broughshane appears in the Royal Belfast Academical Institution school prizes in June 1830 and Belfast College examinations reported in May 1831. The 1831 report also names James Glasgow, Institution, in voluntary advanced mathematical examinations.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 29 June 1830, p.3, Royal Belfast Academical Institution School Department; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390569859/ record]; Belfast News-Letter, 6 May 1831, p.3, Belfast College report dated 30 April; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390545285/ record].</ref> [[Glasgow-1781|Adam Dickie Glasgow]] and James McClure [[Glasgow-1780]] are strong compatible candidates. The newspaper gives no ages or parents and does not call these men brothers. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. Adam D. Glasgow resigned as an assistant in the Royal Belfast Institution’s Mathematical and Mercantile School in December 1836. Rev. Adam D. Glasgow received a unanimous call to Berry Street Presbyterian Church, Belfast, in January 1840 and was its newly ordained minister at a congregational presentation on 5 March.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 10 January 1837, p.2, resignation presentation on 22 December 1836; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390542489/ record]; Belfast News-Letter, 17 January 1840, p.2, Berry Street ministerial call; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390553900/ record]; Belfast News-Letter, 10 March 1840, p.2, Berry Street soiree on 5 March; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390555182/ record].</ref> The repeated name and institutional setting support the education/teaching continuity; the ministerial continuation and attribution to [[Glasgow-1781|Adam Dickie Glasgow]] remain qualified. The newspaper does not spell out Dickie or identify parents. 5 March is the presentation date, not a proved ordination date. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. A marriage notice reports that on 30 December 1841 Rev. Adam Glasgow married Miss Jane Thompson at the house of her uncle, Thomas Corbett, Esq., on May-street. The date 30 December is derived from “30th ult.” in the 4 January issue.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 4 January 1842, p. 3, marriage notice for Rev. Adam Glasgow and Miss Jane Thompson; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390552100/ record].</ref> The notice records Rev. Adam Glasgow as groom and Miss Jane Thompson as bride, married on 30 December 1841 (derived from “30th ult.” in the 4 January 1842 issue). Thomas Corbett is described as the bride’s uncle; no parentage or family branch is stated. May-street identifies the house where the notice says the wedding took place, not Adam’s residence. This is compatible with, but does not prove, identification of the bride as the tree-linked Jane Fulton (Thompson) Glasgow or the groom as [[Glasgow-1781]]. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. A designation report names the Rev. Adam Glasgow among four ministers set apart as missionaries to India and explicitly says he was “brother of the Rev. Jas. Glasgow.”<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 14 January 1842, p. 2, designation of four missionaries to India; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390552341/ record].</ref> The report explicitly describes the named Rev. Adam Glasgow as brother of Rev. Jas. Glasgow. This is a report of the same missionary-designation service also reported by the Freeman’s Journal on 14 January 1842; independence between reports is not assumed. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. An India Mission prayer-meeting notice reports that letters from Rev. Adam Glasgow and Rev. Mr. Spier were read at Rosemary-street Church.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 28 March 1843, p. 2, India Mission prayer meeting and letters; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390560193/ record].</ref> The notice names Rev. Adam Glasgow as a letter author in the India Mission context. It gives no middle name, home locality, or unique identity bridge. The Belfast church is the meeting venue, not a stated residence or congregation for Adam. This is consistent with, but does not uniquely identify, [[Glasgow-1781]]. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. A report of the 10 March 1841 meeting at Rev. Dr. Hanna’s Rosemary-street Church names Rev. Adam Glasgow among the clergy “on and around the platform.” Malone follows Rev. Joseph M’Kenzie, not Adam.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 12 March 1841, p. 3, clergy and deputation meeting/platform report; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390556571/ record].</ref> This report identifies Rev. Adam Glasgow among clergy at the meeting; it does not state his residence or uniquely identify him as [[Glasgow-1781]]. Malone belongs to Rev. Joseph M’Kenzie. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. At the Townsend-street congregational and Sabbath-School soiree on 18 August 1840, devotional exercises were conducted by “the Rev. Adam Glasgow, of Berry-street.” “Of Berry-street” is his printed church association, not proof of residence.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 21 August 1840, p. 2, Townsend-street congregational and Sabbath-School soiree; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390560975/ record].</ref> “Of Berry-street” is the printed church association for Rev. Adam Glasgow, not proof of residence. A separate later passage names Rev. James Glasgow, Missionary to India; this is compatible with [[Glasgow-1780]] but does not uniquely identify him. Their co-occurrence is not evidence of kinship. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. Marriage notice: on 25 July 1840 (reported as “25th ult.”), Mr James Small, of Lottery Cottage, county Armagh, married Miss Margaret Small of this town; the officiant was Rev. Adam Glasgow.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 7 August 1840, p. 3; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390560450/ record].</ref> Minister/officiant occurrence, not kinship. Keep adjacent London/St George’s wedding separate. Strongly compatible with [[Glasgow-1781]], without unique identification. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. Separate soirée passage: at a Tuesday-evening meeting on 27 October at the New School-house connected with the Presbyterian Church, Townsend-street, Rev. Adam Glasgow opened the proceedings; Rev. Josias Wilson closed with prayer.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 30 October 1840, p. 2; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390563103/ record].</ref> Keep both distinct passages in one page row and one clip asset, with Adam as an additional excerpt. Strongly compatible with [[Glasgow-1781]]; no kinship. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. Belfast Town Mission annual meeting in the new school-room, Fisherwick-place, was held “on Wednesday evening last”; Rev. Adam Glasgow is among listed speakers.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 6 November 1840, p. 2; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390563260/ record].</ref> Separate anti-slavery meeting on page is unrelated. A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. General Synod report separately says ordained Ministers Messrs Adam Glasgow and James Carr offered themselves for foreign mission in India and were accepted; initial field Kathiawar/Guzerat, planned departure 4 August overland to Bombay.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 14 July 1840, p. 1; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390559244/ record].</ref> This is James Carr, not James Glasgow in adjacent set-apart report. Planned departure is not proof journey occurred. The identification remains uncertain.

=== Rev A. J. Glasgow’s Belfast speech, 1841 ===

At an entertainment for retiring elocution teacher Robert L. Rogers, held at the Royal Temperance Hotel, Waring Street, Belfast, Rev A. J. Glasgow spoke on 8 April 1841 about elocution for candidates for the sacred ministry. The report also describes classes in Rev Dr Cooke’s church. The initials are printed A. J.; no forename expansion, congregation, age, family or birthplace is supplied.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/390557883/ Belfast News-Letter, 20 April 1841, p.2; report of event on 8 April].</ref>

Adam Dickie Glasgow’s Belfast Presbyterian ministry makes him a compatible speaker, but the printed J. differs materially from his otherwise documented D. The letter was visually distinguished in the original article and is not silently corrected. [[Glasgow-1780|James McClure Glasgow]] was in Bombay with his family in spring 1841 and is strongly disfavoured.
